keyPoint.label: 🔑 Key point
keyPoint.why: Bitcoin moves one asset by one rule; Ethereum runs any rule you can write.
keyPoint.turing: Turing-complete = can compute anything computable, given enough gas.
keyPoint.wallet: A wallet manages keys, not coins: the coins live on-chain and whoever holds the key controls them.
keyPoint.accountsVisual: Only wallets can start a transaction; contracts only react.
keyPoint.evm: Thousands of machines run the same program and must agree on one result.
keyPoint.transaction: Every change on Ethereum starts as a signed message from a wallet, and that wallet pays for it.
keyPoint.gas: Gas prices every step of computation and guarantees every program stops.
keyPoint.eip1559: The network sets the price and burns it; the tip is the only part you negotiate.
keyPoint.smartContracts: Once deployed, a contract gives the same output for the same input, and nobody can quietly edit it.
keyPoint.consensus: Security moved from burning electricity to risking capital.
keyPoint.staking: The return is real, but getting in and out takes time.
keyPoint.issuance: Bitcoin sells scarcity by rule; Ethereum sells scarcity by usage.
keyPoint.evmEcosystem: The EVM is the shared standard: build once, deploy on many chains.
keyPoint.rollups: Rollups move execution off Ethereum while security stays on it.
keyPoint.rollups2: Optimistic rollups wait a week to be sure; ZK rollups prove it up front. Either way users pay cents.
keyPoint.defi: Swap, lend and earn recombine into almost every DeFi product.
keyPoint.stablecoins: A stablecoin is only as stable as what backs it.
keyPoint.apps1: Tokens prove who owns what and who gets to decide.
keyPoint.apps2: Identity and gaming work technically; adoption is the open question.
keyPoint.comparison: Bitcoin is a settlement asset; Ethereum is a settlement platform.
keyPoint.bestFits: Choose Ethereum when composability and shared liquidity are the product.
keyPoint.worstFits: If you don't need programmability or openness, a public chain is a cost, not a feature.

turing.heading: What “Turing-complete” means
turing.subtitle: Bitcoin's scripting language is a fixed menu. Ethereum's machine is a kitchen.

menu.title: Bitcoin Script
menu.tag: A vending machine — like a calculator
menu.body: Press a button, get the matching result. Predictable, and nothing else is possible by design.

kitchen.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine

tools.label: Repeat
tools.desc: Loops — do a step again and again

kitchen.body: Any recipe you can write down, it can cook: an auction, a loan, a token, a voting system.

turing.catchBody: a recipe can also say “repeat forever”. That is why every step costs gas — when the gas runs out, the program stops.

wallet.heading: What a Wallet Actually Is
wallet.subtitle: The app, the key and the address are three different things

layers.label: Seed phrase
layers.detail: The master backup. It regenerates every key in the wallet. Anyone who has it controls the funds.

layers.label: Private key
layers.detail: Signs transactions on your device. The signature proves the account owner approved the action.

layers.label: Address
layers.detail: Derived from the key and safe to share. Others send to it; it cannot be worked back into the key.

appPoints: Your keys, encrypted behind a password
Not your ETH: balances live on the blockchain, the app only reads them
Lose the app and keep the seed phrase: nothing is lost. Lose the seed phrase: nothing is recoverable.
wallet.gasBody: The account that signs the transaction pays the fee in ETH, even when it only calls a contract.

eoa.title: EOA
eoa.subtitle: Externally Owned Account: the wallet you control (MetaMask, Rabby, a hardware wallet)
points: Controlled by a private key (a human or software)
The ONLY type that can initiate a transaction
Holds ETH balance — no code, no storage
eoa.examples: Browser/mobile wallet · Hardware wallet · Exchange hot wallet

contract.title: Contract Account
contract.subtitle: Smart Contract
points: Controlled by code — no private key exists
Can ONLY respond to incoming calls (never initiates)
Has ETH balance + executable code + persistent storage
Gas is paid by the EOA that triggered it
contract.examples: Uniswap pool · USDC token · NFT collection · DAO treasury

eip1559.heading: EIP-1559 — Making Fees Predictable
eip1559.subtitle: London hard fork · August 2021
eip1559.beforeBody: Users guessed how much to bid. The highest fees won block space, so most people overpaid to avoid getting stuck.
eip1559.tipBodyA: Optional. Paid by user, kept by the
eip1559.tipBodyB: . Usually 1–2 Gwei; higher only for urgent inclusion.

whyWorks.rest: wallets show the base fee in real time, so no blind bidding.
burned ETH offsets new issuance, sometimes fully.
validators can't pocket the base fee, so they have no reason to push it up.

steps.label: Deposit
steps.detail: You lock 32 ETH as a security deposit. That deposit is what you stand to lose if you cheat.

steps.label: Propose
steps.detail: Every 12 seconds one validator is picked at random to build the next block.

steps.label: Attest
steps.detail: The other validators check the block and vote on it.

steps.label: Finalize
steps.detail: After enough votes the block is final. Undoing it would mean burning a third of all staked ETH.

staking.subtitleA: Lock ETH as a security deposit, help validate blocks, and earn
staking.subtitleB: in new ETH. Cheat and you get
staking.subtitleC: (part of your deposit is burned). You cannot get in or out instantly.
staking.instructorBody: Ether Capital (Toronto, publicly listed) was one of the first public companies to run its own ETH staking operation, reporting validator yield as a line item.

amountMeaning.1: A small saver — below the 32 ETH minimum for running a validator.
amountMeaning.1000: A treasury or fund — 31 validators' worth.

pathMeaning.solo: Run your own validator: 32 ETH per validator, a machine online 24/7, full rewards and full responsibility.
pathMeaning.liquid: Deposit any amount with Lido or Rocket Pool and receive a tradable token (stETH, rETH) that represents your stake.
pathMeaning.etf: Buy shares of a staked-ETH fund in a brokerage account. US spot-ETH ETFs were cleared to stake in 2025.

can.soloNo: ✗ No — solo staking needs 32 ETH per validator; {{amount}} ETH is below the minimum.
can.soloMany: ✓ Yes — enough for {{validators}} validators (or one large validator since the 2025 Pectra upgrade).
can.liquid: ✓ Yes — any amount. The pool runs the validators; your token keeps earning in your wallet.
can.etf: ✓ Yes — any amount. The fund stakes the ETH and holds the keys, not you.

earnNote.solo: Full rewards. You carry the uptime and slashing risk yourself.
earnNote.liquid: After the pool's ~10% fee. Smart-contract risk; Lido alone holds ≈25–30% of all staked ETH.
earnNote.etf: After the fund's fee. Counterparty and regulatory risk sit with the fund.

sim.exitLabel: How long to get your ETH back

exit.solo: Join the exit queue: hours to weeks, depending on how many others are leaving. Then about a day until the ETH is back in your wallet.
exit.liquid: Sell the token instantly on the market — but when many want out at once it can trade below 1:1 (≈0.94 in June 2022). Redeeming 1:1 takes days.
exit.etf: Sell your shares any trading day; cash arrives the next business day — you never hold ETH. The fund itself waits in the same exit queue, so it keeps part of its ETH unstaked.

liquid: sell instantly, or redeem in days

issuance.heading: ETH Issuance: No Hard Cap, Nearly Flat Supply
issuance.subtitle: Bitcoin's supply follows a fixed schedule. Ethereum's is what the protocol issues minus what it burns.

facts.title: No hard cap
facts.detail: Nothing in the protocol limits total ETH. The policy has changed by upgrade.

facts.title: The Merge cut issuance ~88%
facts.detail: Miners earned ~13,000 ETH/day. Validators earned ~1,700/day right after the Merge (≈2,600 today, rising slowly with the amount staked).

facts.title: EIP-1559 burns the base fee
facts.detail: Every transaction destroys its base fee. Busy network → more burned than issued → supply shrinks (“ultrasound money”).

chart.title: Total ETH supply, 2015 → 2030 (millions of ETH)
chart.footnote: Stylised curve; dashed lines are projections, not forecasts. Quiet network: issuance beats burn, supply drifts up. Busy network: burn beats issuance, supply shrinks. Either way, well under 1% a year.

issuance.btcBody: Fixed 21M · new coins halve every ~4 years (halvings) · nothing is ever burned · last coin ≈2140. Predictable by rule.

rollups.heading: Rollups: Scaling Without New Trust
rollups.subtitleB: batch thousands of transactions off-chain and post one compressed update to L1, inheriting its security.

steps.label: Users transact on L2
steps.detail: Same wallet, same experience. Confirmed in ~1–2 seconds for cents.

steps.label: Sequencer batches them
steps.detail: The rollup's sequencer orders and executes hundreds to thousands of transactions.

steps.label: Compressed data posted to L1
steps.detail: The compressed batch and new state root are posted to Ethereum (as blobs since EIP-4844), so anyone can verify.

steps.label: L1 verifies and finalises
steps.detail: A proof (validity or fraud) tells L1 the batch is correct. Once accepted, the rollup state is as secure as Ethereum.

rollups.securityNoteRest: · execution moved off-chain · data still on-chain

zk.text: L1 verifies math — no challenge needed

rollups.eip4844B: data: a cheap, short-lived lane on L1 for rollups. L2 fees dropped ~10×.

rollups2.subtitle: Optimistic and ZK rollups differ in how L1 checks the batch. Both move fees from dollars to cents.

stablecoins.heading: Stablecoins: the most-used app on Ethereum
stablecoins.subtitle: A token that tracks 1 USD. The key question is what backs the peg. Three answers, three failure modes.

cards.title: Fiat-backed
cards.mechanism: A regulated issuer holds dollars and T-bills 1:1. Deposit fiat to mint, burn to redeem.
cards.risk: The issuer's bank fails. USDC hit $0.87 in March 2023 with $3.3B stuck at Silicon Valley Bank.

cards.title: Crypto-backed
cards.mechanism: Lock ~$150 of ETH in a contract to mint $100. Fall below the ratio and you are liquidated. No issuer.
cards.risk: A crash outruns the liquidators (March 2020). Capital-inefficient by design.

cards.title: Algorithmic & hybrid
cards.mechanism: Peg held by mint/burn incentives or a delta-neutral hedge rather than full reserves.
cards.risk: Confidence breaks and the peg spirals. TerraUSD erased ~$60B in May 2022. No pure algorithmic design has survived.

apps1.heading: Beyond DeFi — Ownership & Governance
apps1.subtitle: Same token standards, different business: proving who owns what, and letting token-holders run a treasury.

cards.title: NFTs & digital ownership
cards.what: A unique token that proves ownership of one thing: art, a ticket, a domain, a music right. The token is on-chain; the file it points to usually isn't.
cards.limit: If the off-chain file disappears, you own a broken pointer. The 2021–22 speculation collapsed; survivors sell utility (tickets, rights, identity).

cards.title: DAOs & on-chain governance
cards.what: A smart contract holds the treasury and only moves funds when token-holders approve a proposal. The code, not a CEO, executes the decision.
cards.limit: Turnout often 1–5%, whales decide, and most “DAOs” delegate to a small core team. Legal status still unsettled.

apps2.heading: Beyond DeFi — Identity & Gaming
apps2.subtitle: Two areas where programmable ownership works but is not yet mainstream.

cards.title: Identity & decentralised social
cards.what: Your wallet becomes your login. ENS gives it a readable name (alice.eth), Sign-In With Ethereum replaces passwords, and Farcaster and Lens put the social graph on-chain so no platform owns your followers.
cards.limit: Niche next to Web2. Wallet + gas onboarding blocks most users; spam and moderation remain unsolved.

cards.title: On-chain gaming & metaverse
cards.sub: Most assets now live on L2s
cards.what: Game items as tokens players own and trade, from normal games with NFT cosmetics to fully on-chain games where every move is a transaction.
cards.limit: Most Web3 games failed on gameplay and unsustainable tokenomics. Studios now go game first, blockchain optional.

items.option2: No hard cap · ~120M, roughly flat (issuance − burn)

bestFits.subtitleA: Ethereum is the default for anything that needs
bestFits.subtitleStrong: programmable state + composability + an open developer ecosystem

items.name: DeFi & on-chain finance
items.why: Protocols interoperate by default. ~$50B locked across L1 and L2.
items.example: Uniswap (DEX), Aave (lending), MakerDAO (DAI), Lido (staking), Curve (stable swaps).

items.name: NFTs & creator economy
items.why: ERC-721 / ERC-1155 are the standards; provenance is built in.
items.example: OpenSea, Blur, Sotheby's on-chain auctions · ENS domains · POAPs · proof-of-attendance.

items.name: DAOs & on-chain governance
items.why: Token-weighted voting, programmable treasuries, transparent proposals.
items.example: Uniswap DAO ($6B treasury), MakerDAO, Arbitrum DAO, Optimism, Gitcoin grants.

items.name: Stablecoins & tokenised RWAs
items.why: Deepest liquidity for USD-backed tokens; institutional RWA issuance (BlackRock, Franklin Templeton).
items.example: USDC, USDT, DAI, RLUSD, PYUSD on Ethereum · BlackRock BUIDL ($2B+ AUM) · Ondo Finance.

worstFits.subtitle: Jobs where open programmability is the problem, not the solution.

items.name: Pure store of value / digital gold
items.why: ETH has no hard cap and its monetary policy has changed by upgrade (Merge, EIP-1559).
items.alt: Use Bitcoin for neutral, scarce, time-tested SoV.

items.name: Private B2B consortia, regulated data
items.why: Mainnet is fully public: unsuitable for KYC data, supplier contracts, health records. Privacy layers add complexity and trust assumptions.
items.alt: Use Hyperledger Fabric · Quorum · R3 Corda for permissioned channels.

items.name: Consumer-grade payments on L1
items.why: L1 finalises in ~12 min and fees spike with demand. Even with L2s, withdrawals and bridges are slow for retail.
items.alt: Use Bitcoin Lightning · Solana · XRPL · Stellar for sub-second payment UX.

items.name: Latency-critical games / real-time apps
items.why: ~12 s blocks on L1, ~1–2 s on rollups: too slow for real-time gaming or live trading, and order-book matching is expensive in gas.
items.alt: Use Solana · Sui · Aptos · purpose-built order-book chains (dYdX v4) for latency-bound apps.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between an Externally Owned Account (EOA) and a Contract Account on Ethereum?
options: EOAs can store ETH; Contract Accounts can only store code and cannot hold a balance.
Contract Accounts can initiate transactions independently; EOAs can only respond when called by a contract.
EOAs are controlled by a private key and can initiate transactions; Contract Accounts are controlled by code and only execute when triggered by an EOA or another contract.
EOAs exist only on Ethereum mainnet; Contract Accounts work across all EVM-compatible chains automatically.
quiz.explanation: An EOA has a private key, can initiate transactions, and pays gas. A Contract Account has no key; it is code that runs only when another account calls it. A contract cannot act on its own schedule, so every transaction on Ethereum ultimately originates from an EOA.

quiz2.question: An EIP-1559 transaction sets maxFeePerGas = 30 Gwei and maxPriorityFeePerGas = 2 Gwei. The current base fee is 25 Gwei. What does the sender actually pay per gas, and where does each part go?
options: 30 Gwei per gas, all of which is paid to the validator who includes the transaction.
25 Gwei base fee (burned, removed from supply) + 2 Gwei tip (paid to the validator) = 27 Gwei per gas. The remaining 3 Gwei of headroom in maxFeePerGas is refunded to the sender.
25 Gwei base fee paid to the validator + 2 Gwei priority fee burned. Total 27 Gwei per gas.
30 Gwei (max fee) + 2 Gwei (priority fee) = 32 Gwei per gas, paid entirely to the validator.
quiz2.explanation: The base fee (25 Gwei) is burned. The tip (2 Gwei) goes to the validator. Effective price is min(maxFeePerGas, baseFee + tip) = min(30, 27) = 27 Gwei per gas; the unused 3 Gwei is never charged. maxFeePerGas is a cap, not a target.

takeaways.title: Section 02 — Key Takeaways
items: Ethereum adds a Turing-complete virtual machine, the EVM, to the blockchain model
Two account types: Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) and Contract Accounts
Smart contracts are programs stored on-chain that execute deterministically when triggered
The Merge (2022) replaced Proof of Work with Proof of Stake, cutting energy use by 99.95% and new issuance by ~88%
Staking pays ~3–4% a year (solo, liquid or via ETFs), but entry and exit go through queues
ETH has no hard cap: PoS issuance minus the EIP-1559 burn keeps supply roughly flat, and busy periods make it deflationary
The EVM is an industry standard; Polygon, Arbitrum, Base and Optimism are EVM-compatible
Bitcoin is digital money; Ethereum is a programmable settlement layer
